entries.title: Framing Effect – when equivalent descriptions lead to different choices
entries.description:
Framing Effect is the tendency for a judgment or choice to change when the same underlying information is described in different ways. A common example is risky choice: people can respond differently when equivalent outcomes are presented as gains rather than losses.

Where can it show up?
- Risk decisions – a sure outcome can feel different when it is described as people saved rather than people lost.
- Product and business communication – an outcome described as 90% success may be evaluated differently from the equivalent 10% failure description.
- AI-assisted decisions – a model or interface can present the same evidence in a positive or negative frame before a person chooses.

A better check
- Rewrite important options in a neutral form and, when useful, show both the gain and loss descriptions.
- Keep the actual outcomes, probabilities, and missing information the same when testing whether the frame changed the choice.
- Record a choice before and after reframing when the decision is important enough to justify the check.
- Do not treat every wording difference as the same framing effect. Risky-choice, attribute, and goal framing are different research traditions, and their evidence is not equally strong.
